subject: Polity
q: The Right to Education was made a Fundamental Right by which Constitutional Amendment?
history: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, after the Supreme Court in Unni Krishnan (1993) read education into Article 21.
discussion: The amendment added Article 21A for children aged 6-14 and simultaneously changed Article 45 into a directive for early childhood care, showing how a court judgment can mature into constitutional text.

wh.what: Free and compulsory education as a fundamental right
wh.who: Parliament, following Unni Krishnan and Mohini Jain judgments
wh.why: Literacy was a constitutional promise stuck in the Directive Principles

status: Implemented through the Right to Education Act, 2009; NEP 2020 now extends the policy focus to ages 3-18.
why_wrong: The 42nd Amendment is remembered for the mini-Constitution changes and Fundamental Duties, not Article 21A.
The 44th Amendment reversed several Emergency-era distortions of civil liberty.
The 93rd Amendment created reservation for OBCs in private educational institutions.
tip: Anchor amendments to their theme: 42nd = duties and mini-constitution, 44th = undoing Emergency, 52nd = anti-defection, 86th = education, 101st = GST.
improve: Build a one-page timeline of amendments 42 to 106 with the article each one touched.
source: Constitution of India, Article 21A; 86th Amendment Act 2002

subject: Polity
q: A Money Bill is defined under which Article of the Constitution?
history: Article 110 defines a Money Bill as one dealing only with taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund, appropriation of money or audit of Union accounts.
discussion: The Speaker certifies a Bill as a Money Bill, and the Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject it, only recommend within 14 days. The certification power was examined in the Rojer Mathew and Mohd. Saeed Siddiqui line of cases.

wh.what: Definition and scope of a Money Bill
wh.who: Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies it
wh.why: Financial legislation must stay with the directly elected House
wh.how: Lok Sabha passes it; Rajya Sabha has 14 days to recommend

status: Live debate: whether the Speaker's certification is final or open to judicial review in limited circumstances.
why_wrong: Article 108 provides for a joint sitting to resolve deadlock between the Houses.
Article 112 is the annual Financial Statement, the Budget.
Article 117 covers financial Bills other than Money Bills.
tip: Learn 108 to 117 as one cluster — joint sitting, Money Bill, Budget, financial Bills, and the Appropriation process all sit together.
improve: Write a table of Money Bill vs Financial Bill (I and II) vs Ordinary Bill with the role of each House.
source: Constitution of India, Articles 108-117

subject: Polity
q: Which writ literally means 'you may have the body' and is used to produce a detained person before the court?
history: Habeas Corpus is a Latin phrase meaning 'to have the body', an ancient common-law remedy against unlawful detention.
discussion: Unlike the other writs, it can be sought against a private person too and is not limited to public authorities. Courts have used it in cases of preventive detention and illegal custody.

wh.who: Any person in custody or a relative on their behalf
wh.why: Personal liberty is the most basic of fundamental rights
wh.how: The detaining authority must justify the detention

status: Remains the primary judicial safeguard in preventive detention cases under Articles 22 and 21.
why_wrong: Mandamus commands a public authority to perform a duty it has refused to perform.
Quo Warranto questions the authority of a person holding a public office.
Certiorari asks a lower court to transfer its record for review.
tip: Memorise writs by their Latin sense: mandamus = we command, quo warranto = by what authority, certiorari = to be certified.
improve: Take one landmark case per writ — for example Maneka Gandhi for personal liberty.
source: Constitution of India, Articles 32 and 226

subject: Polity
q: The Directive Principles of State Policy were inspired mainly by the Constitution of which country?
history: Part IV of the Constitution drew on the Irish Constitution of 1937, which itself had carried forward the Spanish and papal social encyclical tradition.
discussion: The Irish link explains the unusual mix of welfare socialism and Gandhian village industry in Part IV. The US gave us fundamental rights, Ireland gave us the aspirations.

wh.why: To balance individual liberty with social justice

status: Courts increasingly read DPSP together with fundamental rights, as in the right to health and clean environment.
why_wrong: The US contributed fundamental rights and judicial review, not the Directive Principles.
Australia gave the idea of concurrent lists and freedom of trade.
Canada inspired the federation with a strong centre and residuary powers.
tip: Fix one borrowing per country: Ireland DPSP, US FR and judicial review, UK parliamentary system, Canada strong centre, Australia concurrent list, USSR fundamental duties.
improve: Write down three DPSP that have become enforceable rights through judgments.
source: Constitution of India, Part IV

subject: Polity
q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by which amendment, and on whose recommendation?
history: Part IVA, Article 51A, was inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, listing ten duties.
discussion: The 86th Amendment later added an eleventh duty on education of children aged 6-14. Duties remain non-justiciable but are cited by courts while interpreting reasonableness of restrictions.

wh.who: Swaran Singh Committee recommendation
wh.why: The Emergency-era state wanted civic obligation alongside rights

status: Not enforceable directly; Parliament may enact laws to enforce them, as with the flag code and environmental statutes.
why_wrong: The 44th Amendment restored civil liberties after the Emergency and reduced the amending power's reach.
The 52nd Amendment dealt with anti-defection.
The 73rd Amendment created Panchayati Raj institutions.
tip: Group the 42nd Amendment's four big moves: Preamble words, Fundamental Duties, mini-constitution changes to the judiciary, and transfer of education to the concurrent list.
improve: Learn all eleven duties in a single sentence each so elimination questions become easy.
source: Constitution of India, Article 51A

subject: Polity
q: What is the maximum sanctioned strength of the Rajya Sabha?
history: Article 80 caps the Rajya Sabha at 250 members — up to 238 representing States and Union Territories and 12 nominated by the President for special knowledge.
discussion: The fourth Schedule allocates seats among States, and the actual membership stays below the ceiling because seats follow population and State allocation rather than filling every slot.

wh.how: 238 elected indirectly by MLAs plus 12 nominated
wh.why: To give States a voice and provide a revising chamber
wh.when: Members serve six-year terms, one-third retiring every two years

status: Current strength is 245; the 12 nominated seats have occasionally stayed vacant for long periods.
why_wrong: 238 is only the elected component, not the ceiling.
245 is the present actual strength, not the constitutional maximum.
252 is above the constitutional limit and appears nowhere in Article 80.
tip: Separate the ceiling from the actual: Rajya Sabha 250 ceiling, 245 present; Lok Sabha 552 ceiling, 543 present.
improve: Write the composition of both Houses with ceilings, present strength and term lengths in one table.
source: Constitution of India, Article 80 and Fourth Schedule

subject: Polity
q: President's Rule in a State is imposed under which Article?
history: Article 356 allows the President to assume State functions when the constitutional machinery fails, on a report from the Governor.
discussion: The S.R. Bommai judgment of 1994 made the power justiciable, required a floor test where majority was in doubt, and ended the routine misuse of Article 356 during the 1970s and 1980s.

wh.what: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
wh.who: President, on the Governor's report
wh.why: To preserve constitutional governance in the State
wh.how: Proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months

status: Use has fallen sharply after Bommai; proclamations now typically follow loss of majority and a floor test.
why_wrong: Article 352 is the national emergency provision.
Article 360 covers financial emergency, never invoked.
Article 365 covers a State failing to comply with Union directions.
tip: Emergency articles in order: 352 national, 356 State, 360 financial. Remember 3-5-6 as the ladder downward.
improve: Read the S.R. Bommai ratio once and note the three tests the Court laid down.
source: Constitution of India, Article 356; S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)

subject: Polity
q: Which of the following is NOT a constitutional body?
history: NITI Aayog was created by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission, which was also non-constitutional.
discussion: Constitutional bodies derive existence from the Constitution itself, so abolishing them needs an amendment. Statutory bodies need a law, and executive bodies need only a cabinet decision.

wh.what: A policy think tank of the Government of India
wh.who: Created by Cabinet resolution, chaired by the Prime Minister
wh.why: To shift from central planning to cooperative federalism

status: Active; publishes the SDG India Index and Multidimensional Poverty Index, and drives Aspirational Districts.
why_wrong: UPSC is under Article 315.
Finance Commission is under Article 280.
Election Commission is under Article 324.
tip: Sort bodies into three buckets: constitutional (UPSC, EC, FC, CAG, Attorney General), statutory (NHRC, SEBI, RBI), executive (NITI Aayog, Zonal Councils).
improve: Make a 20-row chart of bodies with their source article or Act; this alone covers many prelims questions.
source: Cabinet resolution, 1 January 2015; Articles 280, 315, 324

subject: Polity
q: The Tenth Schedule, dealing with anti-defection, was inserted by which amendment?
history: The 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 added the Tenth Schedule to curb the culture of defection that toppled governments through the 1960s and 1970s.
discussion: The 91st Amendment later removed the one-third split exemption, so only a merger of two-thirds of a legislature party is protected. The Speaker decides disqualification, a role the Supreme Court has repeatedly asked to be time-bound.

wh.who: Speaker or Chairman decides
wh.why: Political instability from floor-crossing

status: Decisional delays by Speakers remain the core criticism; courts have set outer timelines in recent cases.
why_wrong: The 42nd Amendment dealt with the mini-constitution changes.
The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age to 18.
The 91st Amendment limited the Council of Ministers size and removed the split exemption.
tip: Link schedules to numbers: First = States and UTs, Seventh = three lists, Eighth = languages, Ninth = land reform laws, Tenth = defection, Eleventh = Panchayats, Twelfth = Municipalities.
improve: Note three Supreme Court decisions on Speaker delay and the relief granted in each.
source: Constitution of India, Tenth Schedule; 52nd and 91st Amendments

subject: Polity
q: Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment?
history: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble and changed 'unity of the Nation' to 'unity and integrity of the Nation'.
discussion: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended without altering its basic structure. The 42nd Amendment is the only one to have touched the Preamble.

wh.who: Parliament under the 42nd Amendment
wh.why: To formally commit the Republic to socialism and secularism

status: Both words have been interpreted by courts as descriptive of the constitutional scheme, not as a licence for any single economic model.
why_wrong: These three words were in the original 1949 Preamble.
Justice, liberty and equality are original Preamble words.
Fraternity is original; dignity appears in the Fundamental Rights chapter, not the Preamble.
tip: Only one amendment has ever changed the Preamble — the 42nd. Any question offering another number is a distractor.
improve: Recite the Preamble and mark which words are original and which were added in 1976.
source: Constitution of India, Preamble; 42nd Amendment Act 1976

subject: History
q: Where did Gautama Buddha deliver his first sermon, known as the Dhammachakka-pravartana?
history: After enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, the Buddha preached the first sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath, near Varanasi, setting the wheel of law in motion.
discussion: The four sites of the Buddha's life story map neatly onto four events: birth at Lumbini, enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath, and mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar.

wh.what: First sermon and the Four Noble Truths
wh.who: Gautama Buddha to his five former companions
wh.why: To set out the middle path and the eightfold path

status: Sarnath remains an archaeological and pilgrimage site with the Dhamek Stupa marking the event.
why_wrong: Bodh Gaya is the place of enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.
Kushinagar is where the Buddha passed away.
Rajgriha hosted the first Buddhist council after his death.
tip: Attach every event to one site and one council; Buddhist councils are a recurring question set.
improve: Learn the four Buddhist councils with venue, patron and outcome in a four-row table.
source: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History

subject: History
q: The Kalinga war, which turned Ashoka towards Dhamma, is described in which Major Rock Edict?
history: Major Rock Edict XIII records the conquest of Kalinga in the eighth year of Ashoka's reign, around 261 BCE, and his remorse at the slaughter.
discussion: The edict also names five Hellenistic kings as recipients of his Dhamma missions, which is how historians date and locate his diplomatic reach.

wh.what: Account of the Kalinga war and remorse
wh.who: Ashoka Maurya
wh.why: To announce a shift from conquest by arms to conquest by Dhamma

status: Ashokan edicts remain the earliest deciphered Indian inscriptions, read after James Prinsep's 1837 breakthrough.
why_wrong: Rock Edict II mentions medical facilities for men and animals.
Rock Edict X praises Dhamma administration.
Rock Edict XI sets out the policy of Dhamma gifts to all sects.
tip: Remember XIII as the unlucky war edict: thirteen matches the year of the Kalinga campaign in the eighth regnal year narrative.
improve: List five Ashokan edicts with their subject in one column; exams rarely go beyond that list.
source: Major Rock Edict XIII; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part I

subject: History
q: The Permanent Settlement of Bengal was introduced in 1793 by which Governor-General?
history: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793, fixing land revenue in perpetuity with zamindars as the revenue collectors.
discussion: The settlement guaranteed State revenue and created a loyal rentier class, but it also entrenched absentee landlordism and left cultivators without security of tenure.

wh.what: A permanent land revenue system with zamindars
wh.who: Lord Cornwallis
wh.why: To stabilise revenue and create allies for the Company

status: Subsequently moderated by tenancy reforms and abolished formally in independent India by zamindari abolition laws.
why_wrong: Warren Hastings introduced the annual and five-yearly revenue experiments before 1793.
Wellesley built the subsidiary alliance system.
Dalhousie introduced the Doctrine of Lapse.
tip: Pair the three settlements: Permanent (Bengal, Cornwallis), Ryotwari (Madras/Bombay, Munro), Mahalwari (North India, Holt Mackenzie).
improve: Write one line on who lost land under each settlement; that framing answers most questions.
source: NCERT Class XII, Modern India

subject: History
q: Who was the first President of the Indian National Congress in 1885?
history: The INC's first session was held in Bombay in December 1885 with Womesh Chandra Bannerjee as President and 72 delegates; A.O. Hume was the moving force behind its founding.
discussion: The early Congress was a moderate body seeking representation in councils, a phase later challenged by Tilak's extremists and then by Gandhi's mass politics.

wh.who: W.C. Bannerjee presiding
wh.why: To create an all-India political platform

status: The party led the freedom struggle and became the dominant political force in independent India.
why_wrong: A.O. Hume was the founder-organiser, not the first President.
Dadabhai Naoroji was President in 1886, 1893 and 1906.
Badruddin Tyabji was the third President, in 1887.
tip: Distinguish founder, first President and first Muslim President — Hume, Bannerjee, Tyabji.
improve: Keep a list of Congress sessions with year, venue and President for 1885 to 1947 highlights.
source: NCERT Class XII, Modern India; INC records

subject: History
q: The Dandi March of 1930 was launched primarily to protest against which tax?
history: Gandhi walked 240 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi over 24 days in March-April 1930 and made salt at the shore, defying the government monopoly.
discussion: Salt was chosen because it touched every household, making the protest legible to the poorest Indian and turning a local act into a national movement.

wh.what: Civil disobedience against the salt law
wh.who: Gandhi with 78 volunteers at the start
wh.why: The salt tax hit every household regardless of income

status: Commemorated annually as the Dandi March anniversary; the site is a national memorial.
why_wrong: Land revenue was the focus of peasant movements such as Champaran and Kheda.
Income tax was not the issue; the campaign targeted a mass consumption item.
Cloth excise was tied to the boycott of foreign cloth, a different strand of the movement.
tip: For every Gandhian movement, fix the year, place and the specific law — Champaran 1917, Kheda 1918, Khilafat 1919, Non-cooperation 1920, Dandi 1930, Quit India 1942.
improve: Draw a one-page timeline of 1915 to 1947 with one trigger per movement.
source: NCERT Class XII, Modern India

subject: History
q: The slogan 'Do or Die' is associated with which movement?
history: At the Gowalia Tank session of August 1942, Gandhi gave the Quit India call with the slogan 'Do or Die', demanding an orderly British withdrawal.
discussion: The movement saw the arrest of the entire Congress leadership, spontaneous mass action, and the parallel government experiments at Ballia, Tamluk and Satara.

wh.who: Gandhi and the Congress Working Committee
wh.why: The fall of Southeast Asia made British withdrawal look urgent

status: Cited as the final mass upsurge before independence; several local parallel governments are studied as evidence of rural self-rule.
why_wrong: Non-Cooperation 1920-22 was built on boycott and the Tilak Swaraj Fund.
Civil Disobedience 1930 followed the Eleven Point ultimatum.
Swadeshi 1905 was the boycott of partition of Bengal.
tip: Three slogans, three movements: Inquilab Zindabad with 1930, Do or Die with 1942, Jai Hind as the final salute.
improve: Learn the parallel governments of 1942 with their districts.
source: NCERT Class XII, Modern India

subject: History
q: The account 'Indica' was written by which Greek ambassador to the Mauryan court?
history: Megasthenes, ambassador of Seleucus Nicator at Chandragupta Maurya's court, wrote Indica describing society, administration and the capital Pataliputra.
discussion: The original is lost and survives only in fragments quoted by later writers, so historians treat its colourful claims cautiously while still mining them for administration details.

wh.who: Megasthenes
wh.why: To inform the Seleucid court about its eastern neighbour

status: Fragments are used in NCERT and in epigraphy courses as a foreign-eye source on the Mauryas.
why_wrong: Fa-Hien was a Chinese pilgrim of the Gupta period.
Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra, not a foreign account.
Al-Biruni came with Mahmud of Ghazni and wrote on eleventh-century India.
tip: Foreign accounts in order: Megasthenes (Mauryan), Fa-Hien (Gupta), Hiuen Tsang (Harsha), Al-Biruni (Ghaznavid).
improve: Note which foreign account is useful for which period; that alone solves elimination questions.
source: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I

subject: History
q: Which Harappan site is known for its brick dockyard?
history: Lothal in Gujarat, on the Bhogava river near the Gulf of Khambhat, has a trapezoidal basin identified as a dockyard with a sluice gate.
discussion: The dockyard supports the reading that Harappans ran long-distance maritime trade with the Persian Gulf, corroborated by Mesopotamian seals found at the site.

wh.who: Excavated by S.R. Rao in 1955-62

status: A national maritime heritage complex is being developed at Lothal, linking ancient trade to modern shipping history.
why_wrong: Kalibangan in Rajasthan is known for ploughed fields and fire altars.
Dholavira is known for its water management and three-part town plan.
Banawali in Haryana is known for its radial street pattern.
tip: One identifier per site is enough: Lothal dockyard, Dholavira water, Kalibangan ploughed field, Rakhigarhi largest site.
improve: Build a site-to-feature flashcard set of 20 Harappan sites.
source: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History Part I; ASI Lothal

subject: History
q: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 between the English East India Company and the forces of which Nawab?
history: Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey on 23 June 1757 with the help of Mir Jafar's defection, securing Bengal's revenues for the Company.
discussion: Plassey was less a battle than a negotiated betrayal; the revenue surplus of Bengal then funded the Company's expansion across India.

wh.what: Battle that established Company power in Bengal
wh.who: Clive against Siraj-ud-Daulah
wh.why: Bengal's wealth and the misuse of trade privileges

status: Often paired with Buxar (1764) in questions; Plassey began Company rule, Buxar legalised it with the Diwani grant of 1765.
why_wrong: Mir Qasim fought at Buxar in 1764 after being installed by the Company.
Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh was an ally at Buxar.
Alivardi Khan was Siraj-ud-Daulah's grandfather and predecessor.
tip: Plassey 1757 gave power, Buxar 1764 gave legitimacy, Allahabad 1765 gave Diwani. Keep the chain.
improve: Learn the three treaties — Allahabad 1765, Srirangapatnam 1792, Bassein 1802 — with their consequences.
source: NCERT Class XII, Modern India

subject: Geography
q: The Tropic of Cancer passes through how many Indian States?
history: The Tropic of Cancer at 23°30' N crosses eight States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
discussion: The line is used in mapping questions because it neatly divides India into a northern temperate and a southern tropical zone, influencing cropping and monsoon behaviour.

wh.where: Eight States from Gujarat to Mizoram
wh.why: It separates tropical from subtropical climate zones
wh.how: Passes near Bhopal, Ranchi and Agartala

status: A standard prelims fact, frequently combined with questions on the Standard Meridian at 82°30' E.
why_wrong: Six undercounts the line, which also crosses Jharkhand and Tripura.
Seven drops Mizoram, the last State before Myanmar.
Nine is a common overcount; no ninth State touches the line.
tip: Recite the eight in west-to-east order as a chant; add Bihar and Odisha deliberately as the two distractors that do not belong.
improve: Draw India's outline once and mark the Tropic of Cancer and Standard Meridian from memory.
source: NCERT Class XI, India Physical Environment

subject: Geography
q: Which is the highest mountain peak located entirely within Indian territory?
history: Kangchenjunga at 8,586 m on the Sikkim-Nepal border is the highest peak wholly within Indian territory; K2 at 8,611 m lies in territory claimed by India but administered by Pakistan.
discussion: The wording matters in exams. 'Highest in India' has been contested since 1959, while 'highest entirely within India' is settled at Kangchenjunga.

wh.what: 8,586 m peak in the eastern Himalayas
wh.when: First climbed in 1955 by a British expedition
wh.why: It marks the eastern anchor of the high Himalayan wall

status: Kangchenjunga is a protected biosphere and a restricted-access climbing zone with a tradition of stopping short of the summit out of religious respect.
why_wrong: K2 lies in Pakistan-administered territory, though India claims the region.
Nanda Devi at 7,816 m is the highest peak entirely within India after Kangchenjunga.
Nanga Parbat is in Pakistan-administered territory.
tip: Read the qualifier before the options: 'entirely within' changes the answer from K2 to Kangchenjunga.
improve: List the top ten Indian peaks with State and height; note which are on borders.
source: Survey of India; NCERT Class XI

subject: Geography
q: Which river is popularly called the 'Sorrow of Bihar'?
history: The Kosi shifts its course by up to 150 km across north Bihar, and its floods since the 1950s have earned it the name Sorrow of Bihar.
discussion: Heavy silt load from the Nepal hills raises the river bed, so embankments fail and the river avulses into new channels, a textbook case of a shifting braided stream.

wh.what: A north Bihar Himalayan river prone to avulsion
wh.where: Flows from Nepal into the Ganga near Kursela
wh.why: Extremely high silt load and low gradient on the plains
wh.how: Embankments and spurs have contained but not solved flooding

status: The Kosi high dam proposal in Nepal remains unresolved; Bihar continues structural and non-structural flood measures.
why_wrong: The Gandak floods but is not the traditional Sorrow of Bihar.
The Son is a southern tributary and not a flood scourge.
The Ghaghara floods eastern UP more than Bihar.
tip: Two sorrows to keep apart: Kosi for Bihar, Damodar for Bengal (also called the Sorrow of Bengal).
improve: Map the eight north Bihar rivers and their Nepal origins in one diagram.
source: NCERT Class XI, India Physical Environment

subject: Geography
q: Black cotton soil of the Deccan is best described as which soil type?
history: Regur or black soil formed from weathered Deccan trap basalt, is rich in iron, lime and magnesia, and retains moisture well, suiting cotton.
discussion: Its dark colour comes from titanium and humus content, and its self-ploughing behaviour on drying and wetting is a favourite exam detail.

wh.what: Black cotton soil, also called regur
wh.why: Derived from basaltic lava of the Deccan traps
wh.how: High clay content makes it swell and crack

status: Heavily used for cotton and soybean; poor drainage and low nitrogen are its main limits.
why_wrong: Alluvial soil is transported by rivers, found in the northern plains and deltas.
Laterite soil forms in high rainfall leaching zones such as Kerala and Karnataka.
Arid soils occur in Rajasthan and lack humus.
tip: Match soil to parent material: regur from basalt, laterite from leaching, alluvial from river deposits, red soil from crystalline rock.
improve: Prepare a soil table with region, crop and one limitation each.
source: NCERT Class XI, India Physical Environment

subject: Geography
q: Which is the longest river of peninsular India?
history: The Godavari rises at Trimbakeshwar in Maharashtra and runs about 1,465 km to the Bay of Bengal, earning the name Dakshin Ganga.
discussion: It drains Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha, and its delta is a major rice and aquaculture belt.

wh.where: Source in Nashik district, mouth in Andhra Pradesh
wh.why: Large basin area across the Deccan plateau
wh.how: Fed by monsoon rainfall and tributaries such as the Indravati

status: Inter-State water sharing among riparian States remains a live dispute, and Polavaram project is contested.
why_wrong: The Krishna is the second longest peninsular river at about 1,400 km.
The Narmada flows west into the Arabian Sea and is shorter.
The Kaveri is about 800 km and mainly a delta river.
tip: Peninsular length order: Godavari, Krishna, Narmada, Mahanadi, Kaveri.
improve: Learn source and mouth for the five major peninsular rivers in one line each.
source: NCERT Class XI, India Physical Environment

subject: Geography
q: Chilika Lake, India's largest brackish water lagoon, lies in which State?
history: Chilika, on the Odisha coast, is a lagoon separated from the Bay of Bengal by a sand bar, and was designated a Ramsar site in 1981.
discussion: Its salinity fluctuates with the opening and closing of the sea mouth, which drives the lagoon's fishery and its famous Irrawaddy dolphin population.

wh.where: Puri, Khordha and Ganjam districts, Odisha
wh.why: Formed by coastal sediment deposition closing a bay
wh.how: Fed by the Daya, Bhargavi and Makra rivers

status: Eutrophication and shrimp-farm pressure are persistent threats; the sea mouth is dredged periodically.
why_wrong: West Bengal's Sundarbans is a delta, not a lagoon.
Andhra Pradesh has Pulicat on its border with Tamil Nadu, which is smaller.
Tamil Nadu's Pulicat portion is smaller than Chilika.
tip: Lagoon pairs: Chilika in Odisha, Pulicat between Andhra and Tamil Nadu, Vembanad in Kerala.
improve: Mark India's Ramsar sites on an outline map by State.
source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; NCERT Class XI

subject: Geography
q: Which Indian State has the longest coastline?
history: Gujarat's coastline of about 1,600 km, including the Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat, is the longest of any Indian State.
discussion: The indented coast with gulfs, creeks and the Kathiawar peninsula gives Gujarat more than twice the coastline of the next State.

wh.why: Deep inlets and peninsular projections
wh.how: About 1,600 km, roughly 20 per cent of India's total

status: Central to port-led development, with Mundra, Kandla and the Vadhavan project.
why_wrong: Tamil Nadu's coast is about 1,076 km.
Andhra Pradesh's coast is about 975 km.
Maharashtra's coast is about 720 km.
tip: Coastline order: Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra.
improve: Note the nine coastal States and four coastal UTs in order of length.
source: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways; NCERT Class XI

subject: Economy
q: The repo rate is the rate at which:
options: Banks lend to their best customers
RBI lends short-term funds to banks against government securities
Banks lend to each other overnight
history: Repo is a repurchase agreement: the RBI lends against government securities with an agreement to buy them back, making it the policy rate since the LAF was introduced in 2000.
discussion: The reverse repo, now the Standing Deposit Facility, absorbs liquidity. The corridor between them steers the call money rate.

wh.what: RBI's short-term lending rate to banks
wh.who: Monetary Policy Committee sets it
wh.why: It transmits policy to lending and deposit rates

status: The SDF introduced in 2022 replaced the fixed reverse repo as the floor of the corridor.
why_wrong: That is the base rate or MCLR, set by each bank.
That describes the reverse repo or the Standing Deposit Facility.
That is the call money rate, determined by the market.
tip: Repo means RBI gives money, reverse repo means RBI takes money. The direction is the whole answer.
improve: Draw the liquidity corridor with SDF, repo and MSF, and label who borrows from whom.
source: RBI Monetary Policy framework; NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics

subject: Economy
q: Fiscal deficit is best defined as:
options: Total expenditure minus total revenue receipts
Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings
Interest payments as a share of GDP
history: Fiscal deficit measures the government's total borrowing requirement, covering both revenue and capital spending gaps.
discussion: Revenue deficit shows consumption shortfall, while fiscal deficit includes capital spending, which is why a government can run a fiscal deficit to build assets.

wh.why: It shows how much the government must borrow to meet spending
wh.how: Total expenditure minus total receipts other than borrowings
wh.who: Reported by the Controller General of Accounts monthly

status: India's fiscal consolidation path targets a deficit below 4.5 per cent of GDP in the medium term under the FRBM framework.
why_wrong: That would overstate the deficit by ignoring non-debt capital receipts such as disinvestment.
That is the revenue deficit.
That is the interest payments ratio, a debt sustainability indicator.
tip: Remember the family: revenue deficit, effective revenue deficit, fiscal deficit, primary deficit. Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
improve: Compute all four deficits from one set of hypothetical budget numbers.
source: Union Budget documents; FRBM Act 2003

subject: Economy
q: GST was introduced in India through which Constitutional Amendment?
history: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 created the GST Council under Article 279A and gave concurrent taxing powers to the Union and States, effective 1 July 2017.
discussion: GST replaced a web of central and State indirect taxes with a destination-based value added tax, with CGST, SGST and IGST as its three forms.

wh.who: GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister
wh.why: To remove cascading taxes and create one national market

status: A five-year compensation guarantee ended in 2022; rate rationalisation into a simpler slab structure is under discussion.
why_wrong: The 99th Amendment created the NJAC, later struck down.
The 100th Amendment implemented the India-Bangladesh land boundary agreement.
The 102nd Amendment gave constitutional status to the NCBC.
tip: The 101st is GST — remember it as the tax chapter. The 102nd is the Backward Classes Commission.
improve: Learn the GST Council's composition and voting formula, 75 per cent weighted voting with the Union holding one-third.
source: 101st Constitutional Amendment Act 2016; GST Council

subject: Economy
q: NITI Aayog replaced which body, and on what date was it constituted?
history: A Cabinet resolution on 1 January 2015 replaced the Planning Commission with NITI Aayog, ending the era of five-year plan allocations.
discussion: The shift was from directive central planning to a think tank that advises States, with cooperative and competitive federalism as its stated model.

wh.who: Chaired by the Prime Minister, with a Vice-Chairman and CEO
wh.why: Planning Commission's one-size model had outlived its use

status: Publishes the SDG India Index, MPI, and runs Aspirational Districts and Aspirational Blocks programmes.
why_wrong: The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280 and still exists.
The National Development Council still exists as a body of Chief Ministers.
The date and the replaced body are both wrong here.
tip: Two dates to fix: Planning Commission 15 March 1950, NITI Aayog 1 January 2015.
improve: Write the institutional structure of NITI Aayog and three of its indices.
source: Cabinet Resolution, 1 January 2015

subject: Economy
q: Which index is used as the headline measure of retail inflation in India?
history: The Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended CPI-Combined as the nominal anchor, and the RBI Act was amended in 2016 to target CPI inflation at 4 per cent with a 2 per cent band.
discussion: WPI tracks wholesale prices without services, so it lags and misses the household basket; CPI includes services and is the policy target.

wh.who: Compiled by NSO under MoSPI
wh.why: It reflects the household consumption basket
wh.how: Weighted price index across rural and urban centres

status: The monetary policy target is 4 per cent CPI inflation with a tolerance band of 2 to 6 per cent, reviewed every five years.
why_wrong: WPI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser and excludes services.
IIP measures industrial output growth, not prices.
The GDP deflator is the broadest price measure but not used as the policy target.
tip: CPI is the policy anchor, WPI is a supplementary indicator, and the deflator is for national accounts.
improve: Compare CPI and WPI weights for food, fuel and services in a small table.
source: RBI Act amendment 2016; MoSPI CPI releases

subject: Economy
q: The Monetary Policy Committee of the RBI consists of how many members?
history: The six-member MPC was constituted in 2016 under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act: three from the RBI including the Governor, and three appointed by the Central Government.
discussion: The Governor has a casting vote in a tie, and the committee must meet at least four times a year, though it meets bi-monthly in practice.

wh.what: Body that sets the policy repo rate
wh.who: Governor, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer, three government nominees
wh.why: To bring transparency and accountability to rate setting

status: The inflation targeting framework is due for review; the 4 per cent target with a 2 to 6 per cent band has been retained so far.
why_wrong: Four is too small and does not match the statutory composition.
Five would create a permanent tie risk.
Eight would give the government an outright majority.
tip: Six members, three plus three, Governor breaks ties — three facts answer most MPC questions.
improve: Learn the MPC's statutory duties and the escape clause for missing the inflation target.
source: RBI Act, Section 45ZB

subject: Environment
q: Project Tiger was launched in which year?
history: Project Tiger began on 1 April 1973 at Jim Corbett National Park with nine reserves, after the 1972 Wildlife Protection Act gave the legal framework.
discussion: The project moved tiger conservation from sport hunting to habitat management with core-buffer zoning, and the National Tiger Conservation Authority now oversees it.

wh.where: Started at Jim Corbett, now across 50 plus reserves
wh.why: Tiger numbers had collapsed to about 1,800 by 1972

status: The 2022 All India Tiger Estimation placed the population at about 3,682, the largest in the world.
why_wrong: 1972 is the Wildlife Protection Act, the enabling law.
1980 is associated with the Forest Conservation Act.
1992 is when Project Elephant was launched.
tip: Pair year and instrument: 1972 Wildlife Act, 1973 Project Tiger, 1980 Forest Conservation Act, 1992 Project Elephant.
improve: Note the difference between a national park, a sanctuary and a reserve under the 1972 Act.
source: National Tiger Conservation Authority; MoEFCC

subject: Environment
q: The Ramsar Convention deals with the conservation of:
history: Signed at Ramsar in Iran in 1971, the convention is the oldest global environmental treaty, focused on wise use of wetlands; India joined in 1982.
discussion: Ramsar sites in India now number over 80, including Chilika, Keoladeo and Sundarbans, and designation brings monitoring obligations rather than new policing powers.

wh.why: Wetlands were being lost faster than forests

status: India has expanded its Ramsar list sharply since 2019 as part of wetland conservation targets.
why_wrong: Migratory birds are covered by the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS).
Desertification is the UNCCD, signed in 1994.
Ozone substances fall under the Montreal Protocol.
tip: One convention per problem: Ramsar wetlands, CMS birds, UNCCD desertification, Montreal ozone, Basel hazardous waste, CITES trade.
improve: Build a six-row table of environmental conventions with year, place and subject.
source: Ramsar Convention Secretariat; MoEFCC

subject: Environment
q: The Montreal Protocol, aimed at protecting the ozone layer, was signed in which year?
history: The Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987 to phase out chlorofluorocarbons, following the 1985 Vienna Convention and the discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole.
discussion: The Kigali Amendment of 2016 extended the protocol to hydrofluorocarbons, which are not ozone depleting but are potent greenhouse gases.

wh.what: Treaty to phase out ozone depleting substances
wh.why: CFCs were thinning the stratospheric ozone layer
wh.how: Country-wise phase-out schedules with a multilateral fund

status: India phased out HCFC-141b and is implementing the HFC phase-down under the India Cooling Action Plan.
why_wrong: 1985 is the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer, a framework without binding cuts.
1992 is the Rio Earth Summit and UNFCCC.
1997 is the Kyoto Protocol.
tip: Ozone sequence: Vienna 1985, Montreal 1987, Kigali 2016.
improve: Distinguish the ozone regime from the climate regime, UNFCCC 1992, Kyoto 1997, Paris 2015.
source: UNEP Ozone Secretariat

subject: Environment
q: Which was the first Biosphere Reserve established in India?
history: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, spanning Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, was designated in 1986 as India's first under the UNESCO Man and Biosphere programme.
discussion: Biosphere reserves have three zones: core, buffer and transition, and they are not the same as national parks or tiger reserves in legal status.

wh.why: To combine conservation with sustainable use and research

status: India has 18 biosphere reserves, of which 12 are in the UNESCO world network.
why_wrong: Nanda Devi was designated in 1988, the second.
Sundarbans came in 1989.
Gulf of Mannar came in 1989.
tip: Firsts in conservation: first biosphere reserve Nilgiri 1986, first national park Hailey (Jim Corbett) 1936, first tiger reserve Corbett 1973.
improve: List India's biosphere reserves with State and UNESCO status.
source: MoEFCC; UNESCO MAB programme

subject: Environment
q: The Chipko movement of 1973 was primarily associated with:
history: Villagers in Chamoli, Uttarakhand, led by Sunderlal Bahuguna and Gaura Devi, hugged trees to prevent logging, giving the movement its name.
discussion: Chipko linked forest rights to livelihoods and later fed into the 1980 Forest Conservation Act, which restricted diversion of forest land.

wh.who: Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Gaura Devi
wh.why: Commercial felling threatened village fuel, fodder and water

status: Its principles continue in joint forest management and community forest rights under the 2006 Forest Rights Act.
why_wrong: Anti-dam protests are associated with the Narmada Bachao Andolan and Silent Valley.
Groundwater recharge is the work of the Tarun Bharat Sangh and similar groups.
Poaching is addressed by enforcement agencies, not social movements of this kind.
tip: Three movements to keep apart: Chipko for forests, Narmada Bachao for dams, Appiko for forests in Karnataka.
improve: Learn one leader, one State and one outcome for each environmental movement since 1970.
source: NCERT Class XII, Politics in India since Independence
